title: A delayed return pulse can conserve debris orbital energy and angular momentum in a Newtonian ASASSN-14ko test
abstract: We test if orbital energy and angular momentum conservation remove a shared-return-delay explanation for the ASASSN-14ko event clock. A synthetic 70-90-day return pulse can shift by 5.9558 days without a shape change. We construct positive visible and later debris distributions with the same total mass and both orbital moments as the same mass on a 108.44-day core orbit. At a black-hole mass of 1e7 solar masses and a visible pericentre of 30 gravitational radii, 0.01 solar masses in the visible pulse need 5.44e47 erg of added orbital energy. An equal later mass balances it with pericentre changes of 2.70-3.30 parts per million. A fixed common pericentre fails under separated energy bands because the angular momentum versus binding energy relation has strict curvature. A conditional energy-only mass bound is 0.254 times the visible mass for the reference initial hidden mean. All 54 selected grid cases admit bound orbits and pass the moment checks. This is a Newtonian conservation counterexample, not a hydrodynamic model, a measured echo, or evidence for steady orbital decay. Launch physics, stellar structure, internal energy, relativity and a full passage sequence remain untested.

display.caption: Synthetic delayed pulse and later gas that preserve mass and both orbital moments. No measured echo is shown.
